reasoning: Plain form I past, ح is 7. Used for praising a person or speaking well of them.
A nut-shop loan with long aa then long oo. Many Ramallah speakers say kaajoo, spelled كاجو, instead.
Pronounced with a long uu, so the spelling is given its و: كوفية, with shadda on the ي. In Ramallah the same scarf is just as often called a 7aTTa.
beet has the long ee, written with kasra on the ي. ج assimilates the article in Levantine, and jdiid drops its first vowel.
The word for spices is بهارات with ه; the entry spells it with ح, which would be an unrelated word about sailors, so I have corrected the letter in the vowelled form.
Long ee, written as kasra on the ي, and taa marbuta after م is e. One cloud from the collective gheem.
Form II with shadda on ي, keeping the ay here because of the following vowel. م is a moon letter.
3am plus the b-imperfect is the Palestinian progressive. The subject is the understood feminine id-dinye, hence the t- prefix; shita is the Levantine verb for raining.

The hamza is medial after the article, so it is written. The loan's e vowels can only be written i in this scheme. mish maashi, literally not walking, is the normal way to say something is not working.
Form II with shadda on ز. ع is 3.
Long oo and an emphatic z, which the scheme cannot capitalise, so it stays z; the emphasis is why the taa marbuta is a rather than e. Often spelled بوظة.
Feminine of m3allim: the stem vowel drops before the ending, giving m3allme with a doubled l and taa marbuta as e.
Long oo and a glottal ق. Mostly said in the phrase shuroo' ish-shams; for the time of day Palestinians often just say 3a bakkiir.
haad is the Palestinian this. ق is a glottal stop and ص is emphatic. biiji 3alayy, literally does it come on me, is the idiom for fitting, with shadda on the final ي.
ishi is the Palestinian something, with the word-initial hamza seat written as a bare vowel. ط is emphatic T.
Long aa then kasra, ع is 3. Plural shawaari3.
The final ه of the MSA spelling is not pronounced, so for the voice it is respelled فواكي, matching how Ramallah says it.
One syllable, short i. Used both for builder's plaster and for the cast on a broken arm.
The English marks this as formal and that is right: it belongs to forecasts and news, where the ق is kept as q. In conversation a Ramallah speaker says ij-jaw.
Long aa then kasra. Also used for stale bread and, of a person, for being stubborn.
hunaak is said in Palestinian, though the everyday counterpart to hoon is more often hniik or hunaak with a reduced first vowel.
ص is emphatic and ح is 7, giving Sa77teen, the dual of Sa77a. The conjunction is a bare w before the consonant.
Palestinians say Dahr with ض for back, which is how the entry spells it. The b-imperfect of waja3 keeps the long uu, byuuja3, plus the object -ni.
Form VIII, with ذ surfacing as z in urban Palestinian, so it is respelled with ز. The initial vowel is i, not MSA i3tadhara.
Plain form I past, ع is 3. The dough itself is 3ajiin.
